questions.title: Why did the court read MPWA § 181.101 to allow only the Commissioner—not employees—to seek average daily wage penalties?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the interplay between § 181.101(a) and § 181.171, subd. 1. Section 181.171 says an employee can sue for violations and recover 'civil penalties or damages provided for in the section violated,' plus 'other appropriate relief.' Yet the panel holds only the Commissioner can 'charge and collect' the average daily wage penalty in § 181.101(a). Why doesn't § 181.171's broad remedial language let a private plaintiff recover those penalties directly? Is the court applying a specific-controls-the-general canon, or is there some other rule of statutory construction doing the work?

questions.title: How did Milner v. Farmers Ins. Exchange inform the MPWA penalty analysis here?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Milner for the idea that employees can enforce § 181.101 violations but that penalties collected under § 181.101(a) are to be collected by the Commissioner and paid to employees. If Milner acknowledges employees receive the penalty proceeds, why isn't that enough to let employees seek the penalties themselves under § 181.171? What exactly did Milner decide (or not decide) about a private right to demand penalties?

questions.title: Does Article III allow a private plaintiff to pursue MFLSA civil penalties that are payable only to the Commissioner?
questions.question_body: The majority remands to consider mootness and mentions standing must persist, while the concurrence questions whether Laidlaw’s deterrence rationale even applies. What are the key differences between Laidlaw’s federal environmental penalties and Minnesota's MFLSA penalties that might defeat injury-in-fact or redressability for a private plaintiff? Is it constitutionally sufficient that a penalty payable to the state might deter future wage violations against the plaintiff class?

questions.title: What would make the MFLSA penalties claim moot under the voluntary cessation doctrine in this context?
questions.question_body: The court says the penalties claim may be moot if it's absolutely clear Consilio's overtime policy won't recur. What kind of evidence would satisfy that burden (formal policy rescission, sworn declarations, compliance history)? Conversely, what evidence would keep the case live (current policy documents, ongoing projects billed without overtime)? How does the burden of proof operate on remand?

questions.title: Did the panel need to resolve jurisdiction before deciding the MPWA merits under Steel Co.?
questions.question_body: The court reached the MPWA merits but vacated and remanded the MFLSA penalties claim for a jurisdictional determination. Is that sequencing consistent with the prohibition on 'hypothetical jurisdiction'? Is the explanation that the MPWA claim indisputably presented a live controversy (because the penalties, if available, would go to the plaintiff) while the MFLSA penalties claim uniquely implicated Article III, so they could decide one without the other?

questions.title: What is the precise source of a private right to ask a court to impose MFLSA civil penalties payable to the Commissioner?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the parties agree MFLSA statutory penalties are payable to the Commissioner, not Cohen. Under which MFLSA provision does a private plaintiff even have a cause of action to seek a judicial order imposing those penalties (e.g., Minn. Stat. § 177.27, subds. 7–8)? Or are penalties available only in enforcement actions by the Commissioner? How have Minnesota courts characterized a private litigant's role in obtaining these penalties?

questions.title: How did the court determine the standard of review and does de novo apply to these mixed statutory and summary judgment issues?
questions.question_body: The panel states it reviews summary judgment de novo, viewing evidence in the non-movant’s favor. Given the heavy statutory-interpretation component and the parties’ stipulations (including payment of wages and liquidated damages), is there any portion of the district court’s decision that would have received deference (e.g., discretionary rulings), or is it all de novo because it’s purely legal?

questions.title: Why doesn’t § 181.171’s phrase 'other appropriate relief' include penalties available in § 181.101 when the employer violates that very section?
questions.question_body: Section 181.171 says an employer 'is liable for compensatory damages and other appropriate relief,' and also that an employer 'is liable to the aggrieved party for the civil penalties or damages provided for in the section violated.' The court nonetheless limits penalties under § 181.101 to those the Commissioner 'may charge and collect.' Do courts read § 181.171’s 'other appropriate relief' as subject to the specific enforcement allocation of the violated section, and if so, what interpretive principle requires that reading?

questions.title: What exactly did Cohen waive on the MWTA claim, and what’s the Eighth Circuit’s threshold for abandonment on appeal?
questions.question_body: The court affirms dismissal of the MWTA claim, citing failure to develop argument or identify statutory authority for civil penalties. What did Cohen need to do to preserve this issue—identify a particular penalty provision in § 181.032 or elsewhere, or develop a theory for 'other appropriate relief'? How strictly does the Eighth Circuit apply forfeiture/waiver rules under Fed. R. App. P. 28(a)(9)(A)?

questions.title: Could Cohen have obtained the injunctive relief he sought (rescission of the policy) without amending the complaint?
questions.question_body: The panel says new claims must be raised by amended complaint, not opposition briefs. But is changing the form of requested injunctive relief (from one set of injunction terms to 'withdraw the 2019 policy') a new claim or just a different remedy? Are there circumstances under Rule 15(b) (issues tried by consent) or Rule 54(c) (grant relief to which a party is entitled) that would have allowed the district court to consider the revised injunction request at summary judgment?

questions.title: Does styling oneself as a 'private attorney general' affect standing or remedies in federal court for state-law wage claims?
questions.question_body: Cohen’s caption calls him a 'private attorney general.' Does that label have any legal effect on his ability to pursue civil penalties or injunctive relief in federal court, especially when state law reserves certain enforcement tools to the Commissioner? Are there Article III or prudential standing limits on private-attorney-general style claims when the requested remedy benefits the state rather than the plaintiff?

questions.title: What showing is required to demonstrate a continuing personal stake for penalties based on deterrence?
questions.question_body: Assuming Laidlaw’s deterrence rationale could apply, what facts would establish that civil penalties under the MFLSA would redress Cohen’s injury through deterrence (e.g., ongoing employment, likelihood of being subject to the policy again, class-wide exposure)? Does it matter that he has already been paid his individual overtime and liquidated damages?

questions.title: Should the court have certified the MPWA penalty question to the Minnesota Supreme Court?
questions.question_body: Given the tension between § 181.171’s remedial language and § 181.101’s Commissioner-centric penalty mechanism, why didn’t the Eighth Circuit certify the question to the Minnesota Supreme Court? What are the standards for certification from the Eighth Circuit or Minnesota federal district courts, and do Minnesota cases (like Milner or Allan) make the answer sufficiently clear to avoid certification?

questions.title: What happens to attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest if the MFLSA penalties claim is moot?
questions.question_body: The concurrence would also vacate the district court’s rulings on fees, costs, and prejudgment interest. If the MFLSA penalties claim is dismissed as moot on remand, does that affect Cohen’s 'prevailing party' status under fee-shifting provisions of the MPWA/MFLSA? Are fees considered collateral and still reviewable if jurisdiction fails on part of the case?

questions.title: Does Consilio’s 'effective concession' of MPWA/MFLSA violations at oral argument change the Article III analysis?
questions.question_body: The panel notes Consilio effectively conceded statutory violations but says jurisdiction is still a concern for penalties. Can such concessions affect standing or mootness, or do they only remove the merits dispute while leaving the court to decide whether there’s still a live case or controversy over the form of relief (penalties, injunction)?
